## Paper

## Abstract

The challenge of dendrite growth limiting metal battery lifespan, despite extensive chemical composition optimizations for artificial solid electrolyte interphases (ASEIs), necessitates the development of ASEI design routes. Regulating the ASEI crystallographic microstructure offers a promising yet underexplored solution with efficacy uncertainty. Critical issue lies in what is the optimal crystallographic microstructure state. Using the ZnS ASEI in aqueous Zn batteries as a case study, here we report the effects of grain orientation and grain boundary density on the performance of Zn negative electrode. The results reveal the existence of an optimal microstructure state—predominant in-plane (111) orientation coupled with a critical grain boundary density of ~55 μm/μm2—which delivers an 18-fold lifespan extension, and over 3400 cycles with a Coulombic efficiency of 99.92% at 5 mA cm-2, surpassing the efficacy of most chemical composition manipulations. Mechanistically, the (111) orientation integrates higher electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength. As grain boundary density increases to tens of μm/μm2, the enhancement in electrochemical kinetics coincides with compromised mechanical strength, with their trade-off delineating the critical density that maximizes electrode cycling stability. Our findings exemplify an efficient ASEI design route—crystallographic microstructure engineering.

---

## Introduction

Rechargeable metal batteries, such as the aqueous zinc batteries, distinguished by their high energy density and cost-effectiveness, represent a vital safeguard against the impending energy crisis1–3. However, improving reliability and longevity remains a challenge4. One of the cruxes lies in the uncontrollable dendrite growth inherent to metal negative electrodes, which results in reduced Coulombic efficiency (CE) and rapid lifespan deterioration5,6. The development of artificial solid electrolyte interphase (ASEI) has emerged as a potential solution to mitigate this crux, while its efficacy and functional stability in high-rate and long-term cycling services are often limited7. As intended by such service scenes, a robust ASEI is expected to function by concurrently blocking deleterious reactions at the electrode/electrolyte interface, facilitating homogeneous ion transport, and mechanically tolerating deposition-induced interfacial fluctuations, thereby suppressing dendrite growth8,9. Meanwhile, once the ASEI is yielded by dendrite growth-induced stress, it will loss structural integrity and undergo functional degradation. These require ASEI to possess both high electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength, rendering the optimization crucial yet highly complex.

Certainly, the design of ASEIs has garnered significant efforts10. For instance, the hybrid design of ZnF2–Ag ASEI enables the mechanistic integration of reduced nucleation and diffusion barrier, leading to enhanced reaction kinetics11. The introduction of a fluoroethylene carbonate additive in Li anode promotes the formation of a LiF-rich ASEI, which leverages the dendrite suppression effect of LiF12. Such design strategies can broadly be categorized as chemical composition manipulation-based routes, which primarily involve the introduction or doping of functional chemical species13,14. Despite certain degrees of functional improvement realized in some ASEIs, an inherent drawback of this route is the lack of compatibility among different strategies, as the applicability of a chemical additive/dopant is always material-specific. This leads to a dilemma in combining multiple strategies to further improve ASEI performance. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop more efficient and universally applicable ASEI design routes that could complement chemical composition-dependent strategies.

Most ASEIs exhibit stable crystalline structures, with two fundamental microstructural characteristics—grain orientation distribution and grain boundary density (ρGB)15,16. Crystallographic orientation has been suggested to directly affect not only ionic affinity and diffusion behavior17, but also anisotropic strength18. Given that grain boundaries (GBs) serve as both ionic transport sites and deformation agencies, varying ρGB can simultaneously regulate ionic transport kinetics and mechanical strength19,20. These insights suggest that engineering the crystallographic microstructure of ASEI may provide a unique opportunity to manage its electrochemical and mechanical properties, thereby improving the functional stability in suppressing dendrite growth. Accordingly, a possible solution to the above dilemma, i.e., an efficient ASEI design route that avoids chemical composition manipulation, is to regulate the crystallographic microstructure. Unfortunately, this route has not been widely appreciated because of the uncertainty regarding its efficacy and the absence of mechanism-based regulation principles.

Although several studies have examined the crystallographic orientation dependence on ionic diffusion kinetics and reaction activities, thus identifying the ‘optimal’ orientation of ASEIs17,21, an overlooked uncertainty remains: whether such an orientation, favorable for electrochemical kinetics, can simultaneously ensure high mechanical strength. If not, the functional stability of ASEI may also be compromised by the rapid puncturing of pre-grown dendrites22. The ρGB of ASEI, typically ranging from 0.01 to 100 μm/μm2, exhibits a possibly nonmonotonic relationship with the mechanical strength19,20,23. The critical ρGB corresponding to the highest mechanical strength can be readily identified at the transition point from the Hall-Petch regime to the inverse Hall-Petch regime24. However, this critical ρGB is generally misaligned with the requirements of electrochemical kinetics, since the latter demands as high ρGB as possible to ensure rapid ionic diffusion25. Such dependencies of electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength on the microstructural characteristics are intertwined or even mutually exclusive, which may lead to multiple competitive and/or synergistic electro-chemo-mechanical mechanisms that complicate the regulation principles. Thus, specific issues emerge concerning the development of crystallographic microstructure-based ASEI design routes: (i) How does the crystallographic microstructure of ASEI affect its electrochemical and mechanical properties, and subsequent dendrite growth behaviors? (ii) What is the optimal crystallographic microstructure state of an ASEI, and to what extent can it deliver in enhancing electrode cycling stability?

Here, these issues are discussed in a sphalerite-phase zinc sulfide (ZnS) ASEI served in aqueous zinc batteries, as it represents one of the available ASEIs with acceptable ionic conductivity, mechanical toughness, and chemical stability, yet it remains susceptible to dendrite growth26,27. A set of ZnS ASEIs with controllable crystallographic microstructures was synthesized on a bare Zn substrate using pulsed laser deposition. Effects of the crystallographic orientation and ρGB of ASEI on the electrochemical kinetics, mechanical strength, and resultant electrode cycling stability were investigated. Two fundamentals are unveiled accordingly: (i) the ZnS (111) orientation can integrate both higher electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength, making it the optimal orientation, (ii) the opposing trends of electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength with increasing ρGB delineate a critical ρGB,c ~55 μm/μm2 that maximizes cycling stability. The ZnS ASEI with such an ‘ideal’ microstructure, featuring predominant in-plane (111) orientation and ρGB,c, yields an 18-fold lifespan extension in symmetric cells and up to 3400 cycles with a 99.92% CE at 5 mA cm−2. Such efficacy rivals, or even surpasses that achieved by chemical composition-dependent strategies, proving an efficient ASEI design route—crystallographic microstructure engineering.

---

## Results

The optimal crystallographic orientation
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to compare the Zn2+ adsorption behaviors among ZnS(111), ZnS(220), and ZnS(311) crystal facets (Figs. 1a, S1), as these facets exhibit relatively high adsorption propensities28. Zn2+ adsorption on Zn(002), which is the most favorable adsorption facet in the zinc system, was considered as well29. Multiple potential adsorption structures were analyzed to identify the site with the lowest adsorption energy, i.e., the preferentially anchored location of the zinc ion, for each facet. In comparison (Fig. 1a), the ZnS (111) facet displays the lowest adsorption energy (−3.57 eV) and the highest density of the active adsorption site. Meanwhile, a more pronounced differential charge density distribution is observed on the ZnS (111) facet, indicating a strong interfacial interaction with Zn2+. These results suggest that the ZnS (111) facet exhibits the highest Zn2+ affinity and Zn2+-ASEI interfacial stability compared to other facets, highlighting its good electrochemical kinetics.

The polycrystalline nature of commercial Zn electrodes makes it difficult to grow a large-scale single crystal of ASEI with the designated orientation. Here, thus, to systematically examine the impact of preferential ZnS(111) orientation on the physicochemical properties and cycling stability, the pulsed laser deposition technique is employed to synthesize ZnS ASEIs with controllable (111) texture intensity and ρGB. The synthesized samples are named using the ZnS_x_ρ nomenclature, where x represents the (111) texture intensity, categorized as weak texture (WT), moderate-intensity texture (MT), or strong texture (ST). As shown in Fig. 1b, as-synthesized ASEIs exhibit uniform and densified microstructures, which are fundamental for enabling strong mechanical support and efficient physical isolation between the Zn electrode and electrolyte30. Notably, the ρGB (~55 μm/μm2) and layer thickness (~1.5 μm) for the ZnS ASEIs are controlled to be identical, i.e., a set of ZnS_x_55 ASEIs (Fig. S2a, b). Note that the 1.5 μm deposition thickness was chosen to ensure adequate mechanical stiffness and fast ionic transport31. X-ray diffraction patterns reveal that the ZnS_ST_55 exhibit the highest in-plane (111) texture intensity, characterized by a high (111) peak yet negligible (220) and (311) peaks (Fig. 1c). The (111) texture weakens in ZnS_MT_55 ASEI and further in ZnS_WT_55 ASEI. The corresponding (111) pole figures are shown in Fig. 1d. Figure 1e presents the high-resolution atomic image of ZnS_ST_55 ASEI. Obviously, Zn atoms exhibit a hexagonal arrangement, with the lattice distances of 3.83 Å and 3.29 Å for the (1 1 0) and (11 2 ) facets, respectively, confirming the presence of an in-plane (111) orientation as well. This set of ZnS_x_55 ASEIs isolates the (111) texture intensity as the only microstructure variable.

Building upon the disparities in ZnS (111) texture intensity, the electrode cycling stability (ECS) was comparatively investigated. Symmetric cell cycling tests reveal that the ZnS ASEI-based cells exhibit significantly prolonged lifespans compared to the bare Zn (Fig. 2a), validating the intrinsic advantages of ZnS ASEI in mitigating dendrite growth26. The Zn@ZnS_ST_55-based cell displays the longest lifespan (exceeding 1000 h), nearly 14 times that of bare Zn. However, such a lifespan-extension effect deteriorates substantially as the ZnS (111) texture weakens, a trend consistently observed irrespective of the current density or areal capacity (Figs. 2a, S3a, b). To assess the Zn plating/stripping reversibility32, Coulombic efficiencies of the asymmetric cells were measured at varying current densities as well (Figs. 2b, S3c–e). As shown in Fig. 2b, c, stronger (111) texture intensity renders more pronounced enhancements in Zn plating/stripping reversibility with high CE retention. For instance, at 5 mA cm−2, the cycling numbers of the Zn@ZnS_ST_55 cell increase by 10 times compared to those of the Zn@ZnS_WT_55 cell. Moreover, the Zn@ZnS_ST_55 cell always displays the minimum polarization voltage during cycling (Fig. S3f–j), revealing a (111) texture-induced reduction in the energy barrier of Zn2+ nucleation/dissolution. These results collectively elucidate the ZnS (111) texture-dictated ECS performance, i.e., ECS increases monotonically with enhancing (111) texture.

ZnS(111) orientation integrating electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength
Electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength are fundamental factors governing the functional efficacy and stability of ASEI9,33. Here, the effects of ZnS (111) texture intensity on these properties were examined to probe the mechanisms underlying the monotonic ECS-(111) texture relationship. The charge-transfer resistance Rct and reaction activation energy Era are derived from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy tests (Fig. 2d, e). Evidently, Zn@ZnS_x_55 electrodes exhibit much lower electrochemical resistance than that of bare Zn. Intriguingly, Rct and Era decreased dramatically with enhancing ZnS (111) texture and reach a minimum in the Zn@ZnS_ST_55 electrode, indicating higher Zn2+ transport kinetics intrinsic to the ZnS (111) orientation34. The Zn2+ conductivity of the ZnS_ST_55 ASEI is as high as 1.65×10−4 S·m−1, approximately 1.6 times greater than that of the ZnS_WT_55 ASEI (Fig. 2f). These results confirm that the in-plane ZnS (111) orientation facilitates Zn2+ migration and nucleation, imparting higher electrochemical kinetics than other orientations.

A significant increase in the hardness of ZnS_x_55 ASEIs with enhancing (111) texture is revealed by nanoindentation tests (Fig. 2g). This implies that the (111) orientation contributes to improving the yield and mechanical failure threshold of the ASEI. The ZnS_ST_55 ASEI also exhibits the highest positive strain rate sensitivity, indicating that it can more effectively withstand the high internal stress induced by rapid dendrite growth35. During long-term cycling services, the ASEI layer undergoes sustained stress from the interfacial deposition layer (Fig. S4h), thereby experiencing creep-related damage processes36,37. Indentation creep responses with controlled maximum loads and loading rates can simulate the service behavior of ASEIs under different charging states and current density scenarios. As shown in Fig. 2h, i, under any maximum load or loading rate condition, a stronger ZnS (111) texture consistently reduces the creep displacement, with ZnS_ST_55 ASEI displaying the smallest displacement. This trend proves that the (111) orientation of ZnS ASEI has higher creep resistance. Such ZnS (111) texture-imparted high mechanical strength and creep resistance can be attributed primarily to the high elastic modulus and low Schmid factor of the (111) crystal facet (Fig. 2j–l), which improve the elastic limit and reduce the resolved shear stress for defect multiplication, respectively.

Clearly, ZnS (111) orientation integrates high electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength. A comparison of dendrite growth under varying charging areal capacities is presented in Figs. 3, S3k. In contrast to the thriving dendrites in the bare Zn anode, ZnS ASEIs exhibit different degrees of dendrite suppression. Specifically, (111) texture enhancement derives a transition of the dendrite morphology and ASEI damage mode: from densely coupled dendritic clusters and interconnected cracks in the ZnS_WT_55 ASEI, to stunted dendrites at the localized delamination site, and ultimately achieving high structural integrity with negligible dendrites and damage in the ZnS_ST_55 ASEI (Fig. 3a). Figure 3b–e show the surficial altitude fluctuations of electrodes developed at different charging areal capacities, providing quantitative insight into dendrite growth. The ZnS_ST_55 ASEI displays significantly reduced altitude fluctuations, with average dendrite widths (Fig. 3d) and fluctuation amplitudes (Fig. 3e), such as at 4 mAh cm−2, which are ~25.0% of those observed in ZnS_WT_55 ASEI. These results verify that a strong ZnS (111) texture boosts the dendrite-suppression efficacy of the ASEI, reinforcing its structural integrity and functional stability in service, which is responsible for the (111) texture intensity-dictated ECS performance (Figs. 2a–c, S3). Undoubtedly, the improved charge transport kinetics and mechanical damage threshold intrinsic to the (111) orientation constitute the primary electro-chemo-mechanical mechanisms (Fig. 2d–l)33. Herein, a key characteristic of the optimal crystallographic microstructure state—predominant in-plane (111) orientation—of ZnS ASEI can be identified.

The optimal grain boundary density
Building upon the preferential ZnS (111) orientation, the grain boundary density ρGB, another fundamental microstructure characteristic with an as-yet-uncovered regulation principle, is investigated to further refine the optimal crystallographic microstructure state of ASEI. A set of ZnS_ST_ρGB ASEIs with varying ρGB, ranging from 35 μm/μm2 to 100 μm/μm2, is synthesized. This ρGB regime corresponds to a grain size interval of ~95 nm to ~30 nm, which is typical for the microstructure of ASEIs constructed via slurry casting or in situ synthesis methodologies38,39. As compared in Fig. S5, the layer thickness, microstructure compactness, elemental distribution, and strong (111) texture of the ASEIs remain largely consistent, with ρGB emerging as the sole variable.

It is found that the hardness of ZnS_ST_ρGB ASEIs decreases with improving ρGB (Fig. 4a), following the inverse Hall-Petch relationship. Since the consistent grain orientation distribution ((111) texture) leads to an identical elastic modulus across the sample set (Fig. S6a), the observed negative correlation between hardness and ρGB likely arises from GB-mediated deformation mechanisms, such as GB sliding or rotation, activated as dislocations are suppressed by the nanoscale grain size40. One can also find that the mechanical strength is more sensitive to ρGB than to the (111) texture intensity (Figs. 4a, 2g). The prevalence of GB-mediated plasticity usually renders the material susceptible to creep41. The ZnS ASEI is no exception; the larger the ρGB, the lower the creep resistance (Fig. 4b, c), regardless of the maximum load and loading rate.

As shown in Fig. 4d–f, improving ρGB monotonously lowers Rct and Era while boosting Zn2+ conductivity. Meanwhile, the cyclic voltammetry curves of ZnS ASEIs with higher ρGB exhibit larger enclosed areas, higher peak current densities, and lower onset overpotentials, suggesting enhanced Zn plating/stripping kinetics (Fig. 4g). Hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that Zn2+ migration in ASEI occurs mainly along the GB, with the migration rate almost proportional to ρGB (Fig. S7b). These observations confirm a positive correlation between electrochemical kinetics and ρGB, along with the underlying mechanism—GB-mediated ionic transport.

The opposing trends in the dependence of electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength on ρGB complicate the identification of the optimal ρGB for ECS performance. Galvanostatic Zn plating/stripping cycling tests of symmetric cells indeed unveil a non-monotonic dependence of the cycling life on ρGB, with the lifespan initially increasing as ρGB improves, before subsequently decreasing (Figs. 4h, S8a, b). Intriguingly, there exists a critical grain boundary density, ρGB,c ~55 μm/μm2, for the longest lifespans at any current densities. For instance, the cycling time of Zn@ZnS_ST_55-based symmetric cells exceeds 1000 h at 2 mA cm−2 and even over 2000 h at a relatively high current density of 10 mA cm−2. This ρGB,c was further confirmed through CE tests (Figs. 4i, j, S8c–j). The corresponding Zn@ZnS_ST_55||Ti cell always exhibits the highest Coulombic efficiency with minimal efficiency fluctuation, the maximum number of charging/discharging cycles, and the lowest polarization voltage. As an exemplar, at 5 mA cm−2, the ZnS_ST_55 displays over 3400 charging/discharging cycles—double that of ZnS_ST_35 and ZnS_ST_100, alongside a high average CE of 99.92%. Clearly, ρGB,c ~55 μm/μm2 is exactly the optimal ρGB for ECS performance, not by meeting the individual requirements of either electrochemical kinetics or mechanical strength but by balancing the two.

The optimal ρGB balancing electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength
The mutually exclusive dependencies of the electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength on ρGB suggest that ρGB,c is delineated by the trade-off between the ECS contribution factors. To unveil the underlying mechanisms, the evolution of ASEI damage is investigated (Fig. 5a). For the lowest ρGB case (the first subgraph in Fig. 5a), large discretely distributed bump-like Zn protrusions are observed, whereas the residual regions remain damage-free. This implies a highly non-uniform Zn deposition process. Such protrusions will serve as the preferential Zn deposition sites, which exacerbate uncontrollable dendrite growth33. As ρGB increases (the second subgraph in Fig. 5a), huge dendrite protrusions are partially suppressed, supplanted by short crack interaction-induced local delamination and local diffuse dendrite growth. Upon reaching ρGB,c (the third subgraph in Fig. 5a), only a few discrete cracks appear, with no exposed dendrites, indicating effectively suppressed dendrite growth, which is responsible for the improved ECS performance (Figs. 4h–j, S8). The appearance of such an near-ideal morphology signifies two service characteristics of the ASEI enabled by ρGB,c: (i) a homogeneous Zn deposition process to alleviate stress concentration, and (ii) improved yield and damage thresholds to preserve structural integrity and thus functional stability. When ρGB exceeds the ρGB,c (the fourth subgraph in Fig. 5a), however, delamination-induced diffused dendrites destroy the structural integrity of ASEI, with the remaining islands being eroded by dendrites as well, significantly reducing the lifespan and CE (Figs. 4h–j, S8). The altitude contours of ASEIs after varying capacity services are compared in Figs. 5b, S8k, l. The ZnS_ST_55 ASEI exhibits the lowest altitude fluctuation at any charging capacity. In contrast, as ρGB deviates from the ρGB,c, significant fluctuations appear with the development of dendrite peaks. Driven by an inhomogeneous electric field and ionic distribution, dendritic tips are preferred by Zn deposition, which feeds back to promote dendrite growth42. Such a self-catalytic cycle intensifies uncontrollable dendrite growth, accelerating structural damage and thus functional degradation of the anode.

As simulated by molecular dynamics, Zn2+ transport and early-stage deposition are ASEI GB-dependent processes (Figs. 5f, S7). Low ρGB renders limited Zn nucleation sites but a faster growth rate for each nucleus. The growing Zn dendrites have a direct piercing effect on ASEI, and the strength mismatch between them could introduce extra shear interactions (Fig. S4h). These effects collectively yield sparsely distributed yet intense stress concentrations along GBs (Fig. 5c). Although the low-ρGB ASEI exhibit high strength (Fig. 4a–c), discrete long cracks form once local yielding occurs, leading to the development of bump-like dendrite protrusions. Moreover, the broader grain size distribution of the ZnS_ST_35 ASEI is also a potential factor promoting dendrite protrusion formation since it exacerbates nucleation heterogeneity (Fig. S5b). Improving ρGB can increase the uniformity of Zn deposition by providing more transport channels and nucleation sites43. However, excessively high ρGB reduces the mechanical strength, which enables extensive nucleation of short cracks, eventually leading to widespread crack erosion and diffuse dendrites (Fig. 5e). In particular, upon approximating ρGB,c ~55 μm/μm2, there are sufficient GBs for ionic transport and Zn nucleation, and relatively high mechanical damage thresholds are maintained. This represents the optimal trade-off between electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength, providing a unique opportunity to resist both bump-like protrusions and diffused dendrite formations (Fig. 5d), thereby enabling ZnS_ST_55 ASEI to maintain good structural integrity. Another key point worth noting is that the ZnS ASEIs exhibit robust grain structure stability, chemical stability and insolubility during service, with no detectable grain coarsening, phase transformation, or side reactions with the electrolyte (Fig. S2c, d, S9). This makes cracking followed by fragmentation the primary mechanism of ASEI consumption. Minimal mechanical damage endows ZnS_ST_55 ASEI with the lowest consumption rate, thereby enhancing its functional robustness. Thus, herein, another key characteristic of the optimal crystallographic microstructure state of ZnS ASEI—ρGB,c ~55 μm/μm2—is identified.

Crystallographic microstructure engineering for ASEI
The existence and the high ECS-improving efficacy of the optimal ZnS ASEI microstructure state, i.e., predominant in-plane (111) orientation coupled with a critical ρGB,c ~55 μm/μm2, suggest an efficient ASEI design route—crystallographic microstructure engineering. This route advocates regulating the microstructural characteristics according to their impacts on the electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength, and then strategically integrate them. If the impacts of a microstructural characteristic on the electrochemical and mechanical properties are synergistic, as exemplified by that of the ZnS ASEI (111) orientation or texture (the lower part in Fig. 6a), it should be monotonically enhanced. Should the impacts exhibit a trade-off relationship, it is necessary to identify the critical threshold of microstructural characteristic that optimally balances mechanical strength and kinetic performance, as exemplified by the regulation of the ρGB of ZnS ASEI (the upper part in Fig. 6a). Strategically incorporating the optimizations of multiple microstructural characteristics into an ASEI can simultaneously improve ionic transport rate, nucleation homogeneity, and mechanical damage threshold, which helps retain structural integrity and functional stability, thereby peaking the ECS performance (Fig. 6). Note that identifying the optimal ASEI microstructure state should follow the principle—prioritizing characteristics dictated by the material chemical composition, then those dependent on these identified ones (Fig. S10). In the ZnS case, the (111) orientation is intrinsically dictated by its chemical composition and sphalerite-phase lattice, thus necessitating to be identified with priority. While the effect of regulating ρGB may depend on the prevailing crystal orientation and should therefore be determined subsequently. Failure to follow this sequence may yield a pseudo-optimal microstructural state.

For the ZnS ASEIs developed in this study, crystallographic microstructure engineering is successfully implemented in ZnS_ST_55 ASEI, imparting 1.5~10-fold extensions in the lifespans of symmetric cells as compared with those of ZnS ASEIs with no or only partially optimized microstructures (Figs. 2a, 4h). Moreover, there is even an 18-fold lifespan extension relative to bare Zn. The electrode protected by ZnS_ST_55 ASEI demonstrates favorable plating/stripping reversibility across a broad current density range—over 3400 cycles with a 99.92% CE at 5 mA cm−2 and 2600 cycles with a 99.82% CE at even 10 mA cm−2. Such performance enhancement rivals or even exceeds that achieved by chemical composition-dependent ASEI design, electrolyte engineering, ASEI orientation optimization and zinc-host regulation (Fig. 6b). This comparison demonstrates the appreciable efficacy of ASEI crystallographic microstructure engineering in improving ECS performance.

Note that crystallographic microstructure engineering also holds significant potential for application to ASEIs with diverse chemistries across various metal negative electrode systems. This can be supported by the documented experimental cases and/or theoretical analyses in which variations in ASEI microstructure always dramatically affect electrode cycling stability, as summarized in Table S2. Specifically, three fundamentals are shared among these cases. First, a significant extension in electrode lifespan is always achieved at a specific ASEI microstructure state17,21. Second, the underlying mechanisms often involve, directly or indirectly, the principle of ASEI crystallographic microstructure engineering—integrating and balancing electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength44. Third, although most efforts have focused on regulating individual crystallographic microstructural features, cases meeting the first two fundamentals encompass ASEIs with diverse chemistries and applied in various electrode systems, including sulfides, oxides, nitrides, fluorides, or metal-organic complexes, used in Zn, Li, Na, and Mg electrodes (Table S2). These suggest that advancing crystallographic microstructure engineering in more ASEIs—enabling synergistic optimization of key microstructural characteristics through scalable, low-cost processes—holds promise for enhancing the performance of next-generation metal batteries.

## Methods

ASEI fabrication, microstructural and physiochemical characterizations
All chemicals were used directly without any purification treatment. Zinc sulfate heptahydrate (ZnSO4·7H2O, >99.99%) was purchased from Aladdin Chemistry Co., Ltd. High-purity zinc sulfide (ZnS, 99.99%) target was supplied by Hefei Kejing Materials Technology Co., Ltd. Commercial cold-rolling zinc and titanium foils (99.99%, 100 μm thickness), Glass fiber separator (Whatman GF/D, 675 μm thickness) were supplied by Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Co., Ltd. Deionized water (18.2 MΩ cm at 23.5 °C) was generated by DURA Pro 12/24.

Pulsed laser deposition system with a 248 nm wavelength KrF excimer laser was utilized for epitaxial deposition of ZnS layers on a Zn electrode. Before deposition, Zn foil was washed with acetone, deionized water, and ethanol thoroughly. Deposition chamber was evacuated to ~4×10−8 torr for avoiding oxygen pollution. The target-substrate distance was fixed at 5.0 cm, and the laser energy was set as 400 mJ with a 2 Hz pulse frequency. The texture intensity and ρGB of ZnS ASEI were controlled by the modulation of Ar partial pressure (from 2×10−3 to 1×10−1 torr), growth temperature (150~250 °C), and deposition time (0.5~4.0 h). The as-prepared electrode was washed, followed by drying and storing under a nitrogen atmosphere.

The morphology of the ZnS ASEI were observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS Gemini SEM 500). A cross-section polisher (IB-19520 JEOL) was carried out to cut the Zn@ZnS_x_ρGB electrode for an accurate measurement of ASEI thickness. The microstructure and chemical components were characterized by a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM, FEI Talos F200X G2) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy detector under 200 kV. The distribution and mean value of grain size for each ASEI were determined by manually measuring the dimensions of over 350 spatially consecutive grains. The average grain size was validated against that determined by the standard Heyn linear intercept method (ASTM E112-13) to ensure accuracy. Grazing incidence X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Smartlab 9KW) was performed at 6° min-1 (step size: 0.01°) from 5° to 90° with a copper radiation (Cu Kα=1.5418 Å). The pole figures of ZnS coating were characterized on an X-ray diffractometer (Panalytical X’pert mrd), with the scanning azimuthal range from 0° to 360° at each tilt angle (0° to 75°). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) with an Al Kα source (Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) under 12 kV with a 400 μm spot size was performed to examine the chemical state of bare Zn (polished under Ar-ion sputtering at 2 kV) and ZnS ASEIs. Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM, Leica DCM8) was employed to measure the altitude fluctuation of Zn dendrites. To characterize the ASEIs during cycling, the cycled cells were disassembled at 25±0.1 °C and the Zn@ZnS_x_ρGB electrodes were washed to remove the residual electrolyte, followed by drying and storing in glass containers filled with nitrogen atmosphere until transfer for SEM, XRD, XPS, and CLSM analysis.

Electrochemical and mechanical measurements
2 M ZnSO4 dissolved in deionized water was used as electrolyte. Symmetric and asymmetric cells were assembled in coin-type cells (CR-2032) with 150 μL electrolyte. All electrodes employed in the coin-type cells were punched into circular disks with a diameter of 12 mm. The glass fiber separators were prepared as 16 mm diameter circles. Potentiostatic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of symmetric cells was performed over a frequency range of 0.01 Hz to 100 kHz using a voltage amplitude of 10 mV under open-circuit voltage conditions. The reaction activation energy was derived from the Arrhenius equation 1/Rct = A·exp(−Era/RT), where Rct represents the charge-transfer resistance and A, R, and T represent the frequency, gas constant, and temperature, respectively. Cyclic voltammetry was performed with a scan rate of 1 mV s−1 from −0.2 to 1.0 V. Ionic conductivity was tested via a blocking electrode method45. For this test, the ZnS ASEI was deposited onto the Ti foil, followed with EIS measurements were performed with a frequency from 0.1 Hz to 100 kHz. The ionic conductivity was then calculated as σ=L/(Rb·S), where Rb represents the resistance, L denotes the thickness of the ZnS ASEI, and S indicates the contact area. All tests were carried out on an electrochemical station (Reference 3000, Gamry Instruments).

All cycling tests were performed in a climatic/environmental chamber at 25±0.1 °C with Land battery testing systems (CT3002A). Galvanostatic charge/discharge tests of the symmetric cells were performed at 2 mA cm−2 to 2 mAh cm−2, 5 mA cm−2 to 5 mAh cm−2, and 10 mA cm−2 to 1 mAh cm−2. Coulombic efficiency (CE) tests were carried out at varying current conditions (2, 5, 8, and 10 mA cm−2) with a cut-off potential of 0.6 V (vs. Zn2+/Zn) on the asymmetric cells to evaluate the stability and reversibility of the ZnS ASEI. The CE was calculated as follows:

CE = (discharge capacity / charge capacity) × 100% (1)

Nanoindentation tests were performed alternatively under continuous stiffness and quasi-static creep modes, using a Berkovich indenter. To mitigate the interference of zinc substrate surface roughness, Zn foils were electrochemically polished to achieve a mirror-like surface before deposition. To avoid substrate effects, indentation depth remains less than 10% of the coating thickness46. The elastic modulus and hardness were calculated based on the Hay-Crawford model47 and Saha-Nix model48, respectively. The holding time of creep measurements was consistently set to be 60 s.

DFT calculation and MD simulation
The Vienna ab initial simulation package (VASP, version 5.4.4) was adopted for DFT calculations via the projector-augmented wave (PAW) method49,50. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) based on the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) formulation was chosen to describe the exchange-correlation interaction51. The optimized ZnS bulk model with the space group of F-43m and Zn of P63/mmm was adopted for constructing the surface model. Six-layer slabs were cleaved with a vacuum region of 15 Å. An energy cutoff of 450 eV was applied. It was verified that a larger energy cutoff could not produce a more accurate prediction for our calculations. The Monkhorst-Pack scheme k-points grid of 3×3×1 was set for Brillouin zone sampling. The electronic self-consistent field (SCF) convergence criterion was set to 10−6 eV. The criterion for ionic relaxation was set as 10−5 eV for energy convergence, and 0.03 eV Å−1 for residual force convergence. The adsorption energy (Ea) was calculated as:

Ea = EZn-substrate − EZn − Esubstrate (2)

where EZn-substrate, EZn, and Esubstrate represent the energy of Zn adsorbed on the substrate, the energy of a single Zn atom, and the energy of the clean substrate, respectively. The optimized computational models were supplied in Supplementary Data 1. The charge density difference distribution was calculated as:

∇ρ = ρZn-substrate − ρZn − ρsubstrate (3)

where ρZn-substrate, ρZn, and ρsubstrate represent the total charge density of the adsorption structure, the charge density of a single Zn atom, and the charge density of the substrate17,34,52. The VESTA software was utilized for the visualization of adsorption structure and charge density distribution53.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed on nanocrystalline ZnS with varying ρGB using the LAMMPS package54. The Stillinger-Weber interatomic potential was adopted55. Visualization and post-processing of atomic configurations were carried out using Ovito software56. The ZnS models were constructed via the Voronoi tessellation method, implemented within the Atomsk software57. The equal numbers of zinc atoms were controlled to randomly distribute on the ZnS substrate. A hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics optimization was employed to explore energetically favorable adsorption sites and migration pathways for the zinc atom through ZnS. The atomic entropy fingerprint method, a proven approach for effective GB identification58, was adopted to distinguish the grain boundary of ZnS and the zinc-atom migration track. The relevant atomic configurations were supplied in Supplementary Data 2. Checking Supplementary Information for more details on modeling information.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors present a study into suppressing dendrite formation on the zinc metal anode in the context of rechargeable aqueous zinc batteries. The idea centers on using an interfacial layer of ZnS to control the anode’s surface microstructure. They study the relationship of its grain structure to the overall cycling performance of the anode, finding optimal conditions that trade-off between its mechanical and ionic conductivity properties.
The study is interesting and has good analysis. I think it has some decent significance to the field of rechargeable aqueous zinc batteries, although their results cannot directly translate to other rechargeable battery metal anodes without being backed up with significant extra experimental studies (well-beyond the scope of a single paper). Whether this meets the novelty/impact criteria for Nature Comms will be up to the editors based on this assessment.
Some more specific comments:
The title needs to mention the context of aqueous zinc rechargeable batteries. While I appreciate the authors would like to suggest the idea of structural crystallography of the anode interface has broad relevance across all metal anodes, these findings can’t really be taken as universal to all metal anodes on the basis of just the results in this manuscript. It lacks any further studies of other chemistries, or even other artificial interface materials, and the level of studies needed would be more than a doubling of the amount of work already in this submission.
How does the grain structure evolve over repeated cycles? If it doesn't change, why not? If it does, does this have any ramifications for long-term use?
Is there any ZnS dissolution?
Why was ZnS selected as the artificial interface layer?
I appreciate it’s difficult to write in a non-native language! But the writing is not good. A thesaurus has been overused (misused) throughout, and has made it difficult to follow as a result. Sometimes due to poor grammar, or convoluted phrasing, or just incorrect use of a word. Again, I appreciate the authors are likely non-native speakers, but the authors can make it easier for themselves by not feeling the need to use overtly ostentatious language. The paper needs an extensive rewrite to make it readable. Some (of many possible) examples: “... which may render multiple competitive and/or synergistic electro-chemomechanical mechanisms, complexing the regulation principles.” Some of this sentence is fine, but this last bit is not correct. “Certainly, if the impacts are competitive, it is demanded to delineate the threshold of microstructure characteristic that can effectively reconcile the kinetics strength trade-off” is faintly comical in how contrived it is to seem sophisticated. Also, the word "doesn't" appears as an informal contraction in the manuscript.
On page 14, the authors claim “crystallographic microstructure engineering does not involve chemical addition and can be realized in situ during ASEI synthesizing, making this route intrinsically cost-effective and highly practicable.” This is directly contradicted by their own work, where they have to use a pulsed laser deposition technique in order to control the texturing adequately. The authors can’t have it both ways: it is either essential to control the ASEI crystal structure, in which case it will be necessary to use sophisticated thin-film deposition techniques, or making an artificial surface interface is simple, in which case it can be done via a simple in situ electrochemical deposition. Without experimental evidence, I cannot see how they can make their current claim here regarding practicality, and certainly not how it is more practical than simple electrolyte engineering. I think it is fine to broadly argue the merits of artificial anode creation versus electrolyte engineering (which isn’t a particularly new set of insights), but this work doesn’t really address one of the main limits with artificial SEIs, which was not their quality but rather their ease of scalable implementation. PLD isn't exactly industrially practical compared to electrolyte additives. To be honest, I think the whole discussion around figure 6 b is misleading and largely unnecessary, and should just be removed.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a thorough investigation into crystallographic microstructure engineering of artificial solid-electrolyte interphases (ASEIs) to improve the stability of metal anodes. Using ZnS-based ASEIs in aqueous Zn metal batteries as a representative system, the authors tackle the challenge of dendrite suppression by systematically elucidating the relationships among grain orientation, grain boundary density (ρGB), and the resulting electrochemical and mechanical properties of ASEIs. The identification of an optimal microstructure—characterized by a predominant (111) orientation and a critical ρGB,c < 55 μm/μm²—demonstrates significant cycling performance (3400 cycles, 99.92% Coulombic efficiency), marking a notable advancement. The study convincingly argues that crystallographic optimization can outperform traditional compositional modifications, offering a potentially universal ASEI design strategy. This work is of interest and could be considered for publication in Nature Communications after the following critical issues are addressed.
1. The ZnS layer fabricated via pulsed laser deposition (PLD) exhibits a thickness of approximately 1.5 μm. This value substantially exceeds the conventional thickness range of SEIs, which are typically on the order of several to tens of nanometers. Thus, referring to this layer as an “ASEI” may be conceptually misleading. It would be more appropriate to describe it as a modification layer or an interfacial coating.
2. While the ZnS layer with (111) orientation demonstrates superior mechanical robustness, the underlying Zn metal anode is relatively soft and mechanically weaker. The mechanical mismatch at the ZnS/Zn interface could result in uneven stress distribution during cycling, potentially introducing localized stress concentrations (e.g., shear and tensile stresses). These may act as mechanical failure initiation sites on the Zn anode and should be thoroughly evaluated.
3. The manuscript lacks discussion on the chemical stability of the ZnS layer under repetitive Zn plating/stripping. It remains unclear whether the ZnS layer undergoes chemical reactions with the electrolyte or evolves during extended cycling. Addressing this question is crucial for validating the long-term reliability of the engineered interface.
4. To convincingly demonstrate the practical effectiveness of ZnS coatings in suppressing dendritic growth, symmetric Zn//Zn cell testing should be conducted under higher areal capacity conditions. This would better mimic realistic usage scenarios and further validate the claimed performance improvements.
5. A minor issue: Table S1 should include additional critical parameters influencing electrochemical performance, such as electrolyte composition and volume, areal capacity, and depth of discharge. These are essential for enabling proper comparison and reproducibility.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents an impressive story in the exploration of new aSEI design route. Taking the ZnS aSEI served in aqueous zinc batteries as a paradigm, the optimal microstructure state—predominant in-plane (111) orientation coupled with a critical grain boundary density ρGB,c was identified by systematical microstructure modulation. This optimization outperforms most reported chemical composition-dependent aSEI designs, delivering unprecedented effectiveness in dendrite suppression, anode lifespan extension and plating/stripping cycling stabilization. It indicates the emergence of a transformative solution to the long-standing bottleneck of efficacy limitation and cross-strategy incompatibility in conventional aSEI designs. Indeed, having elucidated the mechanisms of how microstructural characteristics affect electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength, a new aSEI design route—crystallographic microstructure engineering—was proposed and rationalized. These findings constitute a respectable progress, with notable innovations in aSEI design concept and anode performance improvement, in the field of rechargeable metal batteries. It can meet the standards of Nature Communications, and is likely to engage both academic and industrial audience in energy science community. I would like to support its publication.
The majority of claims in the manuscript have been well rationalized. But there is still a critical issue which may deserve the authors’ attention. The implementation of crystallographic microstructure engineering in aSEI inevitably involves synergistic optimization of multiple microstructure characteristics. Thus, key questions remain: How does the modulation sequence of different microstructural characteristics affect the outcomes, and what principles on the modulation sequence should be followed to achieve the ‘truly’ optimal microstructure state? Since the optimal state of a microstructure characteristic should be interdependent with others, the coordinated optimization of multiple characteristics therefore must be affected by their modulation sequence. It may attain a fake or artifactual optimal state if the modulation sequence is improper. Just taking the ZnS aSEI as an example: if one first identifies the optimal grain boundary density ρc under a non-(111) orientation, then fixes ρc while searching for the optimal orientation, would the resulting ‘optimal’ microstructure state and anode performances differ from those determined in current work? In this regard, to ensure the reliability and practicality of crystallographic microstructure engineering in aSEIs, it is critical to elucidate the principles of the modulation sequence and interdependencies of multiple microstructure characteristics.
Minor additional suggestions:
(1)Line 189-191: The statement “…the high elastic modulus and low Schmid factor…improve the elastic limit and the resolved shear stress for defect multiplication” is really confusion. Low Schmid factor renders low resolved shear stress on slip plane, thus requiring higher applied stress for defects activity.
(2)Line 70: Non-standard reference formatting.
(3)Line 92: What does “CE” means?
(4)Line 93: Should is be stated as "most chemical composition optimized" or "chemical composition optimized"?
(5)It is suggested to delete the less-used abbreviations, such as “PLD”, to enhance the readability.

### Reviewer 4

This work proposes that the crystallographic structural design of an artificial solid–electrolyte interphase (ASEI) can modulate Zn anode behavior, ultimately achieving enhanced cycling stability. The findings may provide some useful insights into interfacial engineering strategies for Zn-based batteries, which could be published in Nature Communications.
However, several important issues should be addressed as follows:
1) The study demonstrates performance improvement of Zn anodes using a crystallographically tailored ZnS_ST(111)_55 ASEI. However, given the broader claim of ASEI design, the authors should discuss the applicability of this approach to other metallic anodes. Can the same crystallographic design strategy be extended to systems beyond Zn—e.g., Li, Na, or Mg? Some discussion or hypothetical extension would strengthen the conceptual universality.
2) Although the manuscript emphasizes crystallographic microstructural rather than chemical composition-dependent control, it remains unclear whether this crystallographic modulation is effective only for ZnS, or potentially applicable to other compounds. The authors should comment on whether similar performance could be realized using other sulfides or even non-sulfide materials.
3) The ASEI layer in this work is controlled to be ~1.5 μm. Is there a critical thickness threshold? Please discuss how ASEI thickness affects the performance overall.
4) The grain size distributions in Figs. S2 and S5 are central to the argument regarding grain boundary (GB) effects. However, the method used to extract these distributions is not clearly described. Since GBs are central to the discussion, direct and spatially resolved techniques such as EBSD would provide more conclusive insights. Please clarify the current method and consider incorporating more direct microstructural evidence.
5) It is unexpected that a modest increase in ρGB from 35 to 40 leads to doubled cycle life and other performance gains. Meanwhile, Fig. S5b shows that ZnS_ST_35 has a much broader grain size distribution compared to other samples. Since similar ρGB values can achieved with different grain size profiles, please discuss whether the performance improvement is solely attributable to ρGB, or if the size distribution also plays a critical role.
6) How does the ASEI layer evolve during cycling? Are there structural changes (e.g., roughening, cracking, dissolution)? If operando or ex-situ monitoring has been performed (e.g., operando cross-sectional imaging, post-cycling cross-sectional SEM), please present them to support the working mechanism of ASEI clarified in this study.
7) In Fig. 5d, the MC/MD simulations suggest Zn preferentially deposits along GBs in low-ρGB ASEI, while flat Zn deposition occurs underneath the ZnS ASEI in high-ρGB cases. However, these trends seem to differ from some experimental observations. Please clarify the connection and discrepancies herein.
8) In the DFT calculation of adsorption energy, was the charge of adsorbed Zn atom considered? Or simply a neutral Zn atom?

Reviewer #1:
Comments: The authors present a study into suppressing dendrite formation on the zinc metal
anode in the context of rechargeable aqueous zinc batteries. The idea centers on using an
interfacial layer of ZnS to control the anode’s surface microstructure. They study the relationship
of its grain structure to the overall cycling performance of the anode, finding optimal conditions that
trade-off between its mechanical and ionic conductivity properties.
The study is interesting and has good analysis. I think it has some decent significance to the field
of rechargeable aqueous zinc batteries, although their results cannot directly translate to other
rechargeable battery metal anodes without being backed up with significant extra experimental
studies (well-beyond the scope of a single paper). Whether this meets the novelty/impact criteria
for Nature Comms will be up to the editors based on this assessment.
Response: Thank you for the kind comments and suggestions sincerely. The concerns are definitely
solid and helpful, which have been seriously considered. Revisions were made accordingly, as
highlighted using red font in the Revised Manuscript or Revised Supplementary Information.
Comment 1.1: The title needs to mention the context of aqueous zinc rechargeable batteries.
While I appreciate the authors would like to suggest the idea of structural crystallography of the
anode interface has broad relevance across all metal anodes, these findings can’t really be taken
as universal to all metal anodes on the basis of just the results in this manuscript. It lacks any
further studies of other chemistries, or even other artificial interface materials, and the level of
studies needed would be more than a doubling of the amount of work already in this submission.
Response 1.1: Thanks for the constructive suggestion. To accurately encapsulate the main findings and
enhance reader comprehension, the title has been revised as "Crystallographic Microstructure
Engineering for Artificial Solid Electrolyte Interphases toward Ultra-Stable Zinc Anode". While, an
alternative title, "Crystallographic Microstructure Engineering for Artificial Solid Electrolyte
Interphases toward Ultra-Stable Metallic Anode: a paradigm in Aqueous Zn Battery Application", is
also considered but temporarily set aside due to its excessive verbosity. We would be happy to hear
from you if there are any more considerations on the title.
Indeed, the previous manuscript is limited by the lack of extended verification and discussion on
the broad applicability and transferability of the proposed ASEI design route, crystallographic
microstructure engineering, to other metallic anodes. The reviewer's feedback brings this to our
attention. Thank you sincerely for this.

Actually, synergistic regulation of multiple crystallographic microstructural features within a
single ASEI, to the authors' knowledge, remained unexplored prior to this work, while several studies
had reported the optimization of individual microstructural property in specific ASEIs. This insight
offers a potential shortcut for validating the broad applicability of ASEI crystallographic microstructure
engineering, which entails regulating the typical microstructural characteristics to the optimal states
based on the principle of integrating and/or balancing electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength.
Specifically, if there are enough cases in which targeted modulation of individual crystallographic
microstructural feature in a specific ASEI—involving the principle of synergizing or balancing
mechanical strength and electrochemical kinetics—can effectively improve anode performance, the
broad applicability of this design route can be thereby confirmed. In this logic framework, three
fundamentals must be met by the cases. (i) The principle of integrating or balancing mechanical strength
and electrochemical kinetics should be followed or be the underlying mechanism in ASEI's
microstructure modulation. (ii) Significant improvement in anode cycling stability is rendered by the
modulation. (iii) The cases meeting the first two fundamentals must encompass diverse metallic anode
systems such as the ASEIs in Zn, Li, Na, and Mg anodes. Simultaneously engineering multiple
crystallographic microstructural features within a single ASEI, although highly desirable, is not
mandatory.
Guided by this logic, we systematically retrieved the experimental records and theoretical
investigations related to the crystallographic microstructural regulation of ASEIs. The representative
cases are collected in Table S2 (Revised Supplementary Information, Page S22). Surprisingly, a
number of ASEI design cases, involving those served in Zn, Li, Na, and Mg metal anodes, indeed meet
the above fundamentals. For instance, Zhou et al. demonstrate that a highly (001)-orientated Li N ASEI
3
extends the cycling life of Li metal anode by ~1.25-fold compared to the randomly oriented counterpart,
due to the integration of high mechanical modulus and ionic conductivity1. A comparative analysis of
Na₂S ASEIs with controlled grain sizes—as reported by Yu et al. and Yang et al.—reveals that a critical
size of ∼50 nm can markedly improve the cycling stability of Na anode, outperforming coarser
microstructures2,3. Moreover, Fu et al. verifies that the Mg-MOF-74 ASEI with a strong (101) texture
enables a dramatic improvement in the cycling lifespan of Mg anode, which is attributed to the
optimized Mg2+ diffusion kinetics4. These paradigms collectively confirm the broad applicability of
crystallographic microstructure engineering across various metal anode systems.
To address these insights, an additional discussion has been incorporated in the Revised
Manuscript as follows (the last paragraph in Page 14) to validate the broad applicability and
transferability of crystallographic microstructure engineering.
Note that crystallographic microstructure engineering also holds significant potential for
application to ASEIs with diverse chemistries across various metal anode systems. This can be
supported by the documented experimental cases and/or theoretical analyses in which variations in
ASEI microstructure always dramatically affect anode cycling stability, as summarized in Table S2.
Specifically, three fundamentals are shared among these cases. First, a significant extension in anode
2 / 34
lifespan is always achieved at a specific ASEI microstructure state17,21. Second, the underlying
mechanisms often involve, directly or indirectly, the principle of ASEI crystallographic microstructure
engineering—integrating and balancing electrochemical kinetics and mechanical strength44 Third,
although most efforts have focused on regulating individual crystallographic microstructural features,
cases meeting the first two fundamentals encompass ASEIs with diverse chemistries and applied in
various anode systems, including sulfides, oxides, nitrides, fluorides, or metal-organic complexes, used
in Zn, Li, Na, and Mg anodes (Table S2). These suggest that advancing crystallographic microstructure
engineering in more ASEIs—enabling synergistic optimization of key microstructural characteristics
through scalable, low-cost processes—holds promise for enhancing the performance of next-generation
metal batteries.
Comment 1.2: How does the grain structure evolve over repeated cycles? If it doesn't change,
why not? If it does, does this have any ramifications for long-term use?
Response 1.2: The concerns are absolutely insightful. The stability of ASEI grain structure is essential
to ensure low ASEI consumption rate and thus functional sustainability during service. Actually, the
evolutions of grain structure—including the crystallographic microstructure and chemical composition,
and the possible influence on ASEI's functionality have been considered and verified during the
investigation. Specifically, high-resolution microstructural characterization, crystallographic analysis
(via XRD), and chemical composition profiling (via XPS) were conducted at multiple cycling stages,
as partially shown in Fig. S9 (Revised Supplementary Information, Page S16). The results
demonstrate that the current ASEIs, especially the ZnS_ST_55 sample, exhibit exceptional
microstructural and chemical stabilities, which remain almost unchanged during cycling. There are two
key physics behind this. (i) The intrinsic mechanical stability of ZnS grains prevents
mechanochemically driven coarsening or phase transformation, even upon cracking and fragmentation.
(ii) The chemical inertness of ZnS suppresses the chemical reactions with electrolyte, thereby avoiding
side reaction-induced dissolution and/or decomposition.

Comment 1.4: Why was ZnS selected as the artificial interface layer?
Response 1.4: In this work, ZnS is selected as a model material to investigate the crystallographic
microstructure engineering of ASEI design. The primary motivation lies in its potential application in
Zn metal anode, owing to its acceptable ionic conductivity, electronic insulation, high mechanical
strength and chemical stability5-9. Chemical stability encompasses the chemical inertness against side
reaction and good insolubility.
In the Revised Manuscript (the last paragraph of Introduction Section, Page 3), a concise
statement on this point is provided as follows:
"Here, these issues are discussed in a sphalerite-phase zinc sulfide (ZnS) ASEI served in aqueous
zinc batteries, as it represents one of the available ASEIs with acceptable ionic conductivity, mechanical
toughness, and chemical stability, yet it remains susceptible to dendrite growth26,27.".

Reviewer #2:
Comments: This manuscript presents a thorough investigation into crystallographic
microstructure engineering of artificial solid-electrolyte interphases (ASEIs) to improve the stability
of metal anodes. Using ZnS-based ASEIs in aqueous Zn metal batteries as a representative
system, the authors tackle the challenge of dendrite suppression by systematically elucidating the
relationships among grain orientation, grain boundary density (ρ ), and the resulting
GB
electrochemical and mechanical properties of ASEIs. The identification of an optimal
microstructure—characterized by a predominant (111) orientation and a critical ρ < 55
GB,c
μm/μm2—demonstrates significant cycling performance (3400 cycles, 99.92% Coulombic
efficiency), marking a notable advancement. The study convincingly argues that crystallographic
optimization can outperform traditional compositional modifications, offering a potentially universal
ASEI design strategy. This work is of interest and could be considered for publication in Nature
Communications after the following critical issues are addressed.
Response: Thanks for the kind comments. The following concerns are particularly insightful and have
been seriously considered. Revisions were made accordingly, as highlighted using red font in the
Revised Manuscript and the Revised Supplementary Information.
Comment 2.1: The ZnS layer fabricated via pulsed laser deposition (PLD) exhibits a thickness of
approximately 1.5 μm. This value substantially exceeds the conventional thickness range of SEIs,
which are typically on the order of several to tens of nanometers. Thus, referring to this layer as
an “ASEI” may be conceptually misleading. It would be more appropriate to describe it as a
modification layer or an interfacial coating.
Response 2.1: It's exactly an insightful comment.
SEI is generally recognized as an electronically insulating and ionically conducting passivation
layer, acted between the electrode and electrolyte (J. Electrochem. Soc 144, L208 (1997), Peled).
Indeed, the conventional SEIs and ASEIs generally exhibit a thickness of several to tens of nanometers
to maintain efficient ionic transport. However, to the authors' knowledge, neither the original SEI
concept introduced by Peled et al. nor subsequent extensive research has established a definitive
thickness range or provided a clear physical rationale for the thickness threshold (J. Electrochem. Soc
144, L208 (1997); J. Electrochem. Soc 126, 2047 (1979)).
Meanwhile, several leading research groups have recently advanced ASEI thickness to micrometer
scale, motivated by the pursuit of enhanced mechanical stiffness to mitigate dendrite-induced stress
concentration1-6. For instance, Archer's research group (Nat. Energy 3, 889-898 (2018)) engineered a
mechanically stable Langmuir-Blodgett ASEI in thickness of ~2-3 μm, which could not only stabilize
11 / 34
the Li anode but also can be facilely assembled. Zhou's group (Nat. Commun. 15, 3085 (2024))
demonstrated a Li N-rich SEI in thickness of ~5-20 μm, which effectively facilitated interfacial ion
3
transport and simultaneously provide sufficient mechanical stiffness. The research by Lu's group (J.
Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 22456-22465 (2023)) constructed a 1.8 μm-thick gradient SEI with organic-
rich surface (CH OC- and C ) and bottom (ZnF ), integrating the merits of fast ionic diffusion and
2 5 2
mechanical flexibility.
In this study, the thickness of the PLD-deposited ASEI layer was controlled at ~1.5 μm to ensure
sufficient stiffness while maintaining ionic conductivity, thereby enhancing its mechanical damage
tolerance and functional durability. A streamlined explanation on the principle of ASEI thickness
chosen has been added in the Revised Manuscript (the last paragraph in Page 4) as follow: "Note
that the 1.5 μm deposition thickness was chosen to ensure adequate mechanical stiffness and fast ionic
transport31".
The authors think that whether calling it "coating" or "ASEI" does not violate the general
connotation of ASEI in the context of battery technology and can be readily understood by readers. For
example, in the work demonstrating an optimal ASEI thickness at the micrometer scale, Cui's group
interchangeably used the terms "coating" and "ASEI" (e.g., "...there existed an optimal coating
thickness (≈1 µm, 1 mil doctor blade) for the artificial SEI layer...") (Adv. Mater. 29, 1605531 (2017)).
We would appreciate the reviewer's guidance should there be any further considerations on this matter.
Comment 2.2: While the ZnS layer with (111) orientation demonstrates superior mechanical
robustness, the underlying Zn metal anode is relatively soft and mechanically weaker. The
mechanical mismatch at the ZnS/Zn interface could result in uneven stress distribution during
cycling, potentially introducing localized stress concentrations (e.g., shear and tensile stresses).
These may act as mechanical failure initiation sites on the Zn anode and should be thoroughly
evaluated.
Response 2.2: It's a solid suggestion. As schematized in Fig. S4e, the mechanical piercing of dendrites
results in high stress concentration in the ASEI layer. Specifically, the stress concentration arises from
two mechanical effects: the direct piercing effect of dendrite, and the deformation mismatch effect
between dendrite and ASEI. During dendrite nucleation and early growth, the stress concentration
induced by direct piercing scales proportionally with dendrite height due to the elastic interaction with
ASEI. As the dendrite grows, stress concentration increases quickly to yield the soft dendrite, the
interaction with the ASEI transitions to elastic/plastic interaction. Namely the ASEI's strong constraint
makes the dendrite tip yield, while the ASEI remains elastic owing to its high strength. This deformation
incompatibility, manifested as Poisson's ratio difference-induced strain mismatch, introduces extra
shear constraint between them, which intensifies the stress concentration in ASEI. High stress
concertation could trigger mechanical damage in ASEI, featured by crack nucleation, crack propagation
and delamination from the Zn substrate, ultimately compromising the dendrite-suppressing
12 / 34
functionality.

Response 4.8: The charge of adsorbed Zn atom was not considered in the DFT calculations. Actually,
employing a neutral atom in adsorption-energy calculation is a well-established and widely accepted
approach for evaluating SEI layer adsorption behavior. For instance, based on the adsorption calculation
of a neutral Zn atom on both hopeite SEI and bare Zn, Guo et al. demonstrated a much stronger Zn
adsorption capability (binding energy of -2.82 eV) for the former12. Wang et al. simulated the adsorption
of neutral Zn atom on TiO ASEI and Zn surfaces, and unveiled the stronger affinity of TiO (100) facet
2 2
accordingly5. Yuan et al. analyzed the neutral K atom adsorption at the V S and V S /graphene atomic
3 4 3 4
interfaces, confirming that the graphene-V S (020) interface exhibits better adsorption capability13.
3 4
Undoubtedly, incorporating the charge of adsorbed Zn atom might better represent the actual reaction
process. Nevertheless, the key factor governing Zn adsorption is the chemical state and surface
accessibility of the adsorbent's active sites, which are directly dictated by the crystal orientation. For
instance, the ZnS (111) orientation has a higher S-site density compared with other orientations, thereby
enabling superior electrochemical kinetics (Fig. 1a). This suggests that when an adatom is adsorbed
onto a sufficiently large adsorbent surface, adatom's charge may not significantly affect the adsorption
trends across different crystallographic orientations. In other words, adatom adsorption behavior across
various crystal facets can serve as a robust descriptor for identifying the electrochemical kinetics-
preferred orientation of current ZnS ASEI.
Moreover, it must be noted that the VASP framework with plane-wave basis set does not allow
31 / 34
assigning charges to an individual adsorbate; instead, it only allows modification of the total number of
electrons through the NELECT tag, which introduces a homogeneous background charge. This, in turn,
inevitably induces long-range spurious Coulomb interactions between neighboring periodic structures,
thereby compromising the reliability of such calculations—the limitation explicitly acknowledged in
the VASP manual. Nevertheless, we have still made extensive efforts on charged-atom adsorption
calculations, by introducing background charges and considering implicit solvation effect with
VASPsol program14-21. However, the calculations have proved to be computationally intractable and
suffered from severe convergence difficulties, attributable to the inherent methodological limitation
described above.
Importantly, the grain orientation/texture-dependent variation of ZnS ASEI's electrochemical
kinetics that predicted from the adsorption energies of neutral Zn atoms on different crystal facets agrees
well with experimental results (Figs. 2c-d), which validates the simulation approach again. A statement
